Tech-enablement theses by company

Each portfolio company gets a named operating system built mostly from proven vendors plus a thin BSP data layer. The aim is to make earnings look more recurring, predictable and scalable to the next buyer, or, for Thomas Scientific, to raise EBITDA directly (ServiceOS evidence).

Thesis and value by company

Punctual ProsServiceOSBooking rate, pricebook and membership density1.0-2.5$0.88M

Sources: ServiceOS evidence; Portfolio AI-agent plan.

Where evidence is strongest

  • Punctual Pros is the lead case. HVAC booking rates average 38%, versus 59% at shops with 25+ technicians. Pricebook adopters grew tickets 14%, versus 8% for non-adopters (ServiceOS evidence).
  • Public residential comps point to a mid-teens EBITDA margin as the mature target. Growth above installer levels needs recurring service agreements (Public comparables).
  • CET and Frontline rest on PKF and Aventis findings that buyers pay for retention and recurring service. Frontline's entry multiple is already about 12-15x (est.), which limits the room for more expansion (ServiceOS evidence).
  • Thomas Scientific is an EBITDA case, not a multiple case. The benchmarks are Avantor at about 80% digital transactions, and Grainger's digital growth of about 15.6% against about 2% for rep-led sales. Capital structure dominates this exit (ServiceOS evidence).

Caveats

  • The premiums for scaled roll-ups mostly reflect scale and density, not technology. The Champions Group and Sila multiples are press estimates (ServiceOS evidence).
  • All agent values are analyst assumptions and are not de-duplicated. Most metric claims come from vendor case studies (Portfolio AI-agent plan).
  • The Fair Harbor premium range and the full SignalOS and HarborOS theses are cut off in the context. The complete ServiceOS evidence file would fill those gaps.

Next actions

  1. Replace the assumed call, ticket, invoice and member volumes with system-of-record counts for each company, starting with the wave-one agents.
  2. Pull baseline booking rate, average ticket and membership count at Punctual Pros to anchor the ServiceOS case.
  3. Retrieve the full Fair Harbor and BPI theses and premium ranges before any portfolio-wide summary goes out.
  4. Model the Thomas Scientific case as EBITDA and leverage impact rather than multiple expansion.

# Tech-enablement theses by company

Each portfolio company gets a named operating system built mostly from proven vendors plus a thin BSP data layer. The aim is to make earnings look more recurring, predictable and scalable to the next buyer, or, for Thomas Scientific, to raise EBITDA directly (ServiceOS evidence).

## Thesis and value by company

| Company | System | Core thesis | Multiple premium (turns, est.) | Agent value (est., annual) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Punctual Pros | ServiceOS | Booking rate, pricebook and membership density | 1.0-2.5 | $0.88M |
| CET | GridOS | Project work becomes recurring solar/SCADA O&M and NuWave/EV monitoring | 0.5-1.5 | $1.32M |
| Frontline | FirmOS | Ticket work becomes measured security and e-billing revenue-cycle lines | 0.5-1.5 | $3.59M |
| Thomas Scientific | LabOS | Digital transactions and lower cost-to-serve | 0.5-1.0 | $3.84M |
| BPI | SignalOS | Monitoring sold as a product; faster drafting with client confidentiality | 0.5-2.0 | $2.27M |
| Fair Harbor | HarborOS | Fewer returns, less excess inventory | not shown in context | $0.77M |

Sources: ServiceOS evidence; Portfolio AI-agent plan.

## Where evidence is strongest

- **Punctual Pros is the lead case.** HVAC booking rates average 38%, versus 59% at shops with 25+ technicians. Pricebook adopters grew tickets 14%, versus 8% for non-adopters (ServiceOS evidence).
- Public residential comps point to a mid-teens EBITDA margin as the mature target. Growth above installer levels needs recurring service agreements (Public comparables).
- **CET and Frontline** rest on PKF and Aventis findings that buyers pay for retention and recurring service. Frontline's entry multiple is already about 12-15x (est.), which limits the room for more expansion (ServiceOS evidence).
- **Thomas Scientific** is an EBITDA case, not a multiple case. The benchmarks are Avantor at about 80% digital transactions, and Grainger's digital growth of about 15.6% against about 2% for rep-led sales. Capital structure dominates this exit (ServiceOS evidence).

## Caveats

- The premiums for scaled roll-ups mostly reflect scale and density, not technology. The Champions Group and Sila multiples are press estimates (ServiceOS evidence).
- All agent values are analyst assumptions and are not de-duplicated. Most metric claims come from vendor case studies (Portfolio AI-agent plan).
- The Fair Harbor premium range and the full SignalOS and HarborOS theses are cut off in the context. The complete ServiceOS evidence file would fill those gaps.

## Next actions

1. Replace the assumed call, ticket, invoice and member volumes with system-of-record counts for each company, starting with the wave-one agents.
2. Pull baseline booking rate, average ticket and membership count at Punctual Pros to anchor the ServiceOS case.
3. Retrieve the full Fair Harbor and BPI theses and premium ranges before any portfolio-wide summary goes out.
4. Model the Thomas Scientific case as EBITDA and leverage impact rather than multiple expansion.
